definition: Plutocratic means governed by the wealthy, with wealth itself holding the power.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word plutocratic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know plutocratic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The regatta's governing board turned plutocratic years ago — every rule change now waits on the pleasure of the three owners with the deepest keels and deeper pockets.
An unequal society merely has gaps between rich and poor — a long way short of plutocratic, where the gap has been promoted into the government.
A privileged class enjoys the advantages money buys — schools, lawyers, second chances — but privilege stops short of plutocratic until wealth is openly steering the state itself.

Moneyed simply means wealthy — a moneyed family, a moneyed neighborhood — and it stops there. Plutocratic makes the stronger claim: the wealth holds the gavel and writes the rules. A moneyed board becomes a plutocratic one only when its riches start deciding the votes.

Money-driven means steered by profit — a money-driven studio, decision, or season, anywhere at all. Plutocratic is specifically about government: not merely that money motivates, but that the wealthy rule. A yard sale can be money-driven; only a system of power can be plutocratic.

power rising from ordinary people at the bottom
Biographers still argue over exactly when the founder crossed the line into autocrat.
Plutocratic means governed by the wealthy, with wealth itself holding the power.

The gold-rush town's charter never mentioned wealth, but its politics were plutocratic from the first assay: the two men who owned the stamp mill picked the sheriff, and the sheriff collected their debts.
Plutocratic is more precise than 'rich' or 'corrupt' because it names who steers: wealth itself.
A rich town isn't plutocratic until money starts writing the rules — and a plutocratic system can be perfectly legal, which is what its critics find most alarming.
Plutocratic is an accusation with a definition behind it: wealth governs.
Prefer it to vague words like 'corrupt' when the mechanism is money — bought seats, weighted votes, donor vetoes.
Among its unit-mates, the first root decides everything: pluto- (wealth) versus theo- (god) versus olig- (few) versus merit (earned skill).

In her senior thesis, Dara reconstructed how Garnet Gulch, a silver town of four thousand, was governed in the 1890s.
On paper it had a mayor and a town council; in the ledgers, it was plutocratic to the bone.
The three mine owners paid the sheriff's salary directly, chose the council slate each spring, and once recalled a judge for ruling against the company store.
Miners could vote, Dara notes, but every name on the ballot had first been approved at the Silver Exchange Club.
Wealth did not merely influence Garnet Gulch, she concludes; wealth held office there.
